goals: Name the forms of presentation and the parts of a table, and classify tabulated data
Build a table with row and column totals
Draw and read simple, multiple, component and percentage component bar diagrams
Compute the angles of a pie diagram and check that they add up to 360 degrees

slides.heading: Presentation of Data
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how to **arrange** collected data in a **table** and draw them as **bars** and **pies**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: forms of presentation, tables and their parts, classification of data, bar diagrams and pie diagrams
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Collected data are easy to lose in a heap of numbers. Presentation arranges them so that a reader can see the story quickly. In this part we learn the forms of presentation, the parts of a table, how data are classified, and how bar diagrams and pie diagrams are drawn from figures that we compute ourselves.

slides.heading: Forms of presentation
slides.body_md: Data can be presented in **words**, in a **table** or in a **diagram**.

rows: Suits a few figures; can explain
Many figures are hard to follow
Exact figures, easy comparison and totals
A long table tires the eye
Pattern is clear at a glance
Exact values are hard to read

visual.alt: Table comparing textual, tabular and diagrammatic presentation on what each is, its merit and its limit

slides.narration: There are three forms of presentation. Textual presentation writes the facts in sentences, and it suits a handful of figures. Tabular presentation puts the figures in rows and columns, which gives exact values and easy totals. Diagrammatic presentation draws bars, pies and graphs, so the pattern is clear at a glance, though exact values are harder to read.

slides.narration: Here is an imagined table of crop output in a district called Devgarh. At the top are the table number and the title. Then comes the unit of measurement. The headings across the top are the captions, and the headings down the left side are the stubs. The figures form the body. Below the table sit the source note and a footnote.

slides.heading: Parts of a table: standard meanings
slides.body_md: Learn the eight parts and the job of each.

rows: A serial number that lets the text refer to the table
A short statement of what the data are, where and when
The unit in which the figures are expressed
A line saying where the figures were obtained
A note explaining a particular entry or exception

visual.alt: Table of the eight parts of a table with the standard meaning of each: table number, title, captions, stubs, body, unit of measurement, source note and footnote

slides.narration: The table number lets the text refer to the table. The title says what the data are, where and when. Captions head the columns, and stubs head the rows. The body holds the figures. The unit tells us how the figures are measured. The source note says where the figures came from. A footnote explains a particular entry or an exception.

slides.heading: Quick check: rows and columns
slides.body_md: Fill in the blanks about the headings of a table.
slides.narration: Think about which headings run across the top and which run down the left side. Each has its own name. Write the name for row headings first, then the name for column headings.

slides.heading: Classification of tabulated data
slides.body_md: A table can group data by an **attribute**, a **measured variable**, **time** or **place**.

rows: An attribute that cannot be measured
Workers of a mill grouped by trade
Workers grouped by monthly wage class
Mill output for each year from 2018 to 2024
Mill output in each of three towns

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of classification of tabulated data, qualitative, quantitative, temporal and spatial, each with an imagined example from a mill

slides.narration: Tabulated data are classified in four ways. Qualitative classification uses an attribute that cannot be measured, such as the trade of a worker. Quantitative classification uses a measurable variable, such as wage classes. Temporal classification arranges data by time, such as year by year. Spatial classification arranges them by place, such as town by town.

slides.heading: Quick check: which classification?
slides.body_md: Households grouped by units of electricity used each month. Which classification is this?
slides.narration: Ask what the households are being grouped by. Is it an attribute, a measured quantity, a period of time or a place? Choose the matching kind of classification.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: totals of a table
slides.body_md: An imagined district, Devgarh, has three blocks. Build the row and column totals of its crop table.
bullets: Step 1 — Add each **row**: wheat 42 + 36 + 20 = 98; rice 30 + 45 + 36 = 111.
Step 2 — Add each **column**: North block 42 + 30 + 12 + 16 = 100.
Step 3 — The **grand total** from the row totals is 98 + 111 + 35 + 56 = 300.
Step 4 — Check: the column totals 100 + 120 + 80 also give **300**.

visual.alt: Table of crop output of the imagined district of Devgarh in thousand tonnes with row totals 98, 111, 35, 56, column totals 100, 120, 80 and grand total 300
visual.caption: Imagined Devgarh district, thousand tonnes: the row totals and column totals both add to the grand total.

slides.narration: Add each row to get its total, for example the wheat row adds to 98. Add each column too, for example the first block adds to 100. The row totals give a grand total of 300. As a check, the column totals must give the same grand total. If they differ, there is an arithmetic slip somewhere.

slides.heading: Bar diagrams: the rules
slides.body_md: In a **bar diagram** the bars have **equal width** and **equal gaps**, so only the **height** carries meaning.

slides.narration: A simple bar diagram draws one bar for each item. The bars are equally wide and equally spaced, so the only thing that changes from bar to bar is the height, and the height shows the value. Here the bars show the total output of four crops in the imagined district. Bars start from a common zero line.

slides.narration: To recap. Data can be presented in words, in tables and in diagrams. A table has a number, title, captions, stubs, body, unit, source note and footnote. Data are classified as qualitative, quantitative, temporal or spatial. Bar diagrams have equal widths and gaps, and only the height matters. In a pie, each angle is the share of the total times three hundred and sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the **parts of a table** and say what each one shows.
For a pie, write the formula first, then work out every angle, and **check that they add to 360°**.
Say why bars need **equal width and equal gaps**.
For a percentage bar, divide by the **bar's own total**.
Always give a **title, labelled axes and units** to a diagram.
slides.narration: A few tips. When asked about a table, name its parts and say what each does. For a pie, write the formula, compute each angle, and check that they add to three hundred and sixty. Explain that bars have equal width and gaps so that only height matters. In a percentage bar, divide by that bar’s own total. And always give a title, labelled axes and units.

slides.heading: Histogram or bar diagram?
slides.body_md: A **histogram** is a set of **adjacent rectangles** for a **continuous** series: no gaps, and **area** proportional to frequency.

rows: Area, and so height when classes are equal

visual.alt: Table comparing a bar diagram with a histogram on data, gaps, what carries the value and width

slides.narration: A histogram is drawn for a continuous series, where one class ends exactly where the next begins. So the rectangles touch, with no gaps. In a histogram the width means something, because it is the class width, and the area of each rectangle is proportional to its frequency. A bar diagram has none of these features.

sections.heading: 1. Forms of presentation and the table
sections.body_md:
Collected data can be presented in three forms: **textual** (in sentences), **tabular** (in rows and columns) and **diagrammatic** (in pictures and graphs). A few figures can be written in words; many figures are best put in a table; a pattern is best shown in a diagram.

A good table has eight parts. The **table number** and **title** identify it; the **unit of measurement** says how the figures are expressed; **captions** head the columns and **stubs** head the rows; the **body** holds the figures; the **source note** says where they came from; a **footnote** explains an entry or exception.

Worked case (imagined district of Devgarh, thousand tonnes): the row totals are 98, 111, 35, 56, the column totals are 100, 120, 80 and the grand total is 300 both ways.

key_terms.definition_md: The arrangement of data in rows and columns.
The heading of a column of a table.
The heading of a row of a table.
The part of a table that holds the figures.
A line below a table saying where its figures were obtained.
A note below a table that explains a particular entry or exception.

sections.heading: 2. Classification of tabulated data
sections.body_md: Tabulated data are classified in four ways. **Qualitative** classification groups items by an attribute that cannot be measured in numbers (trade, gender). **Quantitative** classification groups them by a measurable variable, usually in class intervals (wage classes). **Temporal** classification arranges data by time (year by year). **Spatial** classification arranges them by place (town by town). One table can use more than one: a table of output by year and by town is both temporal and spatial.

key_terms.definition_md: Grouping by an attribute that cannot be measured numerically.
Grouping by the size of a measurable variable.
Grouping by time periods.
Grouping by places or regions.

sections.heading: 3. Bar diagrams
sections.body_md:
In a **bar diagram** the bars have **equal width** and **equal gaps** and start from a common zero line, so only the **height** carries meaning. A **simple bar diagram** shows one series. A **multiple (grouped) bar diagram** shows two or more related series side by side. A **component (sub-divided) bar diagram** divides each bar into parts that make up its total. In the **percentage component bar diagram** every bar is 100 per cent, so the shares of unequal totals can be compared.

Imagined Devgarh: block totals 100, 120, 80; rice share = rice ÷ block total × 100, which is 30%, 37.5%, 45% for the three blocks.

key_terms.definition_md: A diagram with one bar for each item of a single series.
A diagram with grouped bars, one for each of several related series.
A diagram whose bars are divided into the parts of each total.
A component bar diagram in which every bar stands for 100 per cent.

sections.heading: 4. Pie diagrams
sections.body_md:
A **pie diagram** is a circle divided into sectors whose angles are proportional to the shares of the components.

**Angle of a sector = (value of the component ÷ total) × 360°.** The angles add up to **360°**. In the imagined Rao family budget of Rs 24,000 the angles are food 144°, housing 90°, education 54°, transport 36°, health 18°, other items 18°, and their sum is 360°.

A pie suits a few components of one total. With many small sectors, or when two totals are to be compared, a bar diagram is easier to read.

key_terms.definition_md: A circle divided into sectors with angles proportional to the shares of the components.
The part of a circle between two radii.

sections.heading: 5. Histogram, frequency polygon and frequency curve
sections.body_md:
A **histogram** shows a continuous frequency distribution as **adjacent rectangles with no gaps**; the **area** of each rectangle is proportional to its frequency. If the classes have equal widths the heights are the frequencies. If the widths are unequal use the **adjusted frequency = (frequency ÷ class width) × standard width**, taking the lowest width as the standard: for the imagined Kishan Brick Kiln the adjusted frequencies are 12, 20, 18, 8.

A **frequency polygon** is drawn by plotting **class marks against frequencies** and joining them with straight lines (the mid-points of the tops of the rectangles), closed at both ends at the class marks of an imaginary class of zero frequency. A **frequency curve** is a smooth curve through the same points.

key_terms.definition_md: A diagram of adjacent rectangles whose areas are proportional to the frequencies of a continuous series.
The frequency of a class divided by its width and multiplied by a standard width.
A figure obtained by joining the points of class marks and frequencies by straight lines.
A smooth curve drawn through the points of a frequency polygon.

sections.heading: 6. Ogives
sections.body_md: An **ogive** is a cumulative frequency curve. The **less than ogive** plots less than cumulative frequencies against the **upper limits**; the **more than ogive** plots more than cumulative frequencies against the **lower limits**. The two curves cross at the **median**: for the imagined Anand Bolt Works (80 days) they meet at a cumulative frequency of 40 and a daily output of 85 crates, which is the same as the formula L + ((N/2 − cf) ÷ f) × h.

key_terms.definition_md: A curve of cumulative frequencies plotted against class limits.
An ogive of less than cumulative frequencies, plotted against upper limits.
An ogive of more than cumulative frequencies, plotted against lower limits.

questions.stem_md: In a table of weekly sales of the imagined Ravi Cycle Mart, the headings written at the top of the vertical columns, such as Week 1, Week 2 and Total, are called

options.text_md: stubs
captions
body
footnotes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** captions. Column headings are the captions. Stubs are the row headings at the left, the body holds the figures, and a footnote is a note placed below the table.

questions.stem_md: A table lists Gents cycles, Ladies cycles and Kids cycles down its left-hand side, one name for each horizontal row. These labels are the

options.text_md: captions
source note
unit of measurement
stubs

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** stubs. Row headings written down the left side are stubs. Captions head the columns, the source note says where the figures come from, and the unit says how the figures are measured.

questions.stem_md: Which title is best for a table of tomato arrivals at the imagined Pushpa Mandi?

options.text_md: Monthly arrivals of tomatoes at Pushpa Mandi, January to June (in quintals)
Tomato table
Pushpa Mandi
Figures of arrivals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Monthly arrivals of tomatoes at Pushpa Mandi, January to June (in quintals). A good title tells what the data are, where and when they apply, and in what unit. The other titles leave out one or more of these and would not let a reader understand the table on its own.

questions.stem_md: Below a table of daily wages in the imagined Surajpur Brick Works there is the line: Source: Surajpur Brick Works wage register. This line is the

options.text_md: footnote explaining an exception
caption
source note
title

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** source note. A line that tells where the figures were obtained is the source note. A footnote explains a particular entry or exception, a caption heads a column and the title describes the whole table.

questions.stem_md: A table gives the number of students enrolled each year from 2018 to 2024 in the imagined Sagar College. The classification of these data is

options.text_md: spatial, because the data are arranged by place
qualitative, because the data are arranged by an attribute
temporal, because the data are arranged by time
quantitative, because the data are arranged by class intervals of a size

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** temporal, because the data are arranged by time. When data are arranged by time periods such as years, the classification is temporal. Spatial means by place, qualitative by an attribute such as trade or gender, and quantitative by a measurable size such as income.

questions.stem_md: A table lists the July rainfall recorded in the imagined Lakeview, Hillcrest and Rivergate blocks of one district. This is

options.text_md: spatial classification
temporal classification
qualitative classification
quantitative classification

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** spatial classification. The rows differ by place, so the classification is spatial (geographical). Nothing here is arranged by time or by an attribute, and the blocks are not classes of a measurable size.

questions.stem_md: Households of the imagined Madhav Nagar are grouped by monthly electricity use into 0 to 100 units, 100 to 200 units and 200 to 300 units, and the number of households in each group is given. The classification is

options.text_md: qualitative
temporal
spatial
quantitative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** quantitative. Grouping by the size of a measurable variable, here units used, is quantitative classification. Qualitative classification uses attributes that cannot be measured, such as occupation, and the other two use time and place.

questions.stem_md: The three forms in which collected data can be presented are

options.text_md: primary, secondary and tertiary
textual, tabular and diagrammatic
census, sample and pilot
simple, multiple and component

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** textual, tabular and diagrammatic. Data can be written in sentences (textual), arranged in rows and columns (tabular) or drawn as pictures and graphs (diagrammatic). The other sets name kinds of data, methods of enquiry, or kinds of bar diagram.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined district of Devgarh, rice output in the North, Central and South blocks is 30, 45, 36 thousand tonnes. The row total shown for rice in the table is

options.text_md: 111 thousand tonnes
75 thousand tonnes
81 thousand tonnes
300 thousand tonnes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 111 thousand tonnes. A row total adds all the entries of the row: 30 + 45 + 36 = 111. 75 leaves out the South block, 81 leaves out the North block, and 300 is the grand total of all crops.

questions.stem_md: In a simple bar diagram of yearly rainfall in the imagined Meghnad region, the information is carried by

options.text_md: the width of each bar only
the height of each bar only
both the height and the width of each bar
the colour of each bar

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the height of each bar only. All bars have the same width, so only their height (or length) shows the value. Width and colour are chosen for looks and should not be read as data.

questions.stem_md: While drawing a bar diagram of pulses output for five imagined districts, the bars should be drawn

options.text_md: with width proportional to the output
touching each other with no gaps
with equal width and equal gaps between them
with different gaps so that larger bars stand out

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** with equal width and equal gaps between them. Equal width and equal gaps keep the eye on the heights. Bars that touch are the mark of a histogram, and bars of unequal width would give a false impression of size.

questions.stem_md: The owner of an imagined tailoring shop wants to compare, month by month for six months, the number of shirts stitched with the number of trousers stitched. The most suitable diagram is

options.text_md: a pie diagram
a histogram
a less than ogive
a multiple (grouped) bar diagram

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a multiple (grouped) bar diagram. Two related series over the same months are compared side by side in a multiple bar diagram. A pie diagram shows the parts of one total, and a histogram and an ogive are for frequency distributions of a continuous variable.

questions.stem_md: In a component (sub-divided) bar diagram of crop output of the imagined Devgarh district, each bar is cut into parts. The parts show

options.text_md: the same total repeated in different colours
the frequencies of class intervals
the change in the total over time
the components that make up the total shown by the whole bar

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the components that make up the total shown by the whole bar. A sub-divided bar shows the total as the full bar and its components as stacked segments. The segments are not repeated totals, and they are not class frequencies.

questions.stem_md: A percentage component bar diagram of the three blocks of Devgarh differs from the ordinary component bar diagram because

options.text_md: every bar is divided into equal parts
the bars are drawn touching each other
every bar has the same height, and its parts show shares as percentages of that bar's total
the heights of the bars show the totals of the blocks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** every bar has the same height, and its parts show shares as percentages of that bar's total. In the percentage form every bar stands for 100 per cent, so the shares of unequal totals can be compared directly. Equal parts would show nothing, touching bars belong to histograms, and the bar heights no longer show totals.

questions.stem_md: The angle at the centre of a sector in a pie diagram is found as

options.text_md: (value of the component ÷ total) × 100°
(value of the component ÷ total) × 360°
(total ÷ value of the component) × 360°
value of the component × 360°

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** (value of the component ÷ total) × 360°. A sector's share of the circle must equal the component's share of the total, and the full circle is 360 degrees. The other expressions do not give an angle in proportion to the share.

questions.stem_md: An imagined family spends Rs 4,800 on transport out of a monthly budget of Rs 24,000. In a pie diagram the sector for transport has an angle of
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 72°. Angle = (4800 ÷ 24000) × 360° = 72°. 20° is the share in per cent mistaken for degrees, 36° halves the angle and 144° doubles it.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a genuine limitation of a pie diagram?

options.text_md: It cannot show the share of a component in the total
It is hard to read and compare sectors when there are many small components
It can be drawn only for data in percentages
It needs the components to add up to more than the total

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It is hard to read and compare sectors when there are many small components. With many thin sectors a pie becomes crowded, and sectors of near-equal size are hard to compare. A pie does show shares, can be drawn from absolute values by converting to angles, and its components must add up exactly to the total.

questions.stem_md: A histogram of the weights of 60 parcels at the imagined Kulwant Post Office has rectangles standing side by side without gaps because

options.text_md: all the frequencies are equal
the class widths have been chosen at random
a histogram needs less space than a bar diagram
the classes are continuous, with the upper limit of one class equal to the lower limit of the next

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the classes are continuous, with the upper limit of one class equal to the lower limit of the next. A continuous variable has no break between classes, so the rectangles touch. Frequencies need not be equal, class widths are chosen on purpose and saving space is not the reason.

questions.stem_md: In a histogram of the imagined Kishan Brick Kiln wages, one class is twice as wide as the lowest class. For the areas of the rectangles to stay proportional to the frequencies, the height for that class must be

options.text_md: its frequency divided by its width, multiplied by the lowest width (the adjusted frequency)
its frequency, without any change
its class mark
its cumulative frequency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** its frequency divided by its width, multiplied by the lowest width (the adjusted frequency). In a histogram area, not height, represents frequency. A wide class would look too large if its raw frequency were used, so its frequency is spread over a standard width. Class marks and cumulative frequencies are not heights of a histogram.

questions.stem_md: A frequency polygon drawn over the histogram of daily output of the imagined Anand Bolt Works is obtained by joining

options.text_md: the upper-right corners of the rectangles with a smooth curve
the lower limits of the classes
the mid-points of the tops of the rectangles with straight lines
the centres of the bases of the rectangles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the mid-points of the tops of the rectangles with straight lines. The polygon joins the points whose x values are the class marks and whose heights are the frequencies, which are the mid-points of the tops of the rectangles. Joining corners or base centres does not give that figure, and a smooth curve would be a frequency curve.

questions.stem_md: To complete the frequency polygon so that it forms a closed figure with the horizontal axis, the polygon is extended at each end to

options.text_md: the origin of the graph
the highest frequency
the class mark of an imaginary class with zero frequency
the median class

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the class mark of an imaginary class with zero frequency. An imaginary class with zero frequency is added before the first and after the last class, and the line is brought down to its class mark on the axis. The origin and the median class have no role in closing the figure.

questions.stem_md: To draw a less than ogive, the cumulative frequencies are plotted against

options.text_md: the upper limits of the classes
the lower limits of the classes
the class marks
the class widths

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the upper limits of the classes. A less than cumulative frequency counts the items below an upper limit, so it is paired with that upper limit. Lower limits are used for the more than ogive.

questions.stem_md: For the waiting times of the 50 patients of the imagined Rajpur clinic, the point to be plotted for the class starting at 15 minutes on the more than ogive is (15, 15). The 15 stands for

options.text_md: patients who waited less than 15 minutes
patients who waited exactly 15 minutes
the frequency of the class 15 to 20
patients who waited 15 minutes or more

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** patients who waited 15 minutes or more. A more than point at a lower limit counts all items at or above it: 50 − 35 = 15. 35 is the less than figure at 15, and the frequency of the class 15 to 20 is 10, not 15.

questions.stem_md: When the less than and more than ogives of a series are drawn on the same graph, the value of the variable at the point where they intersect is the

options.text_md: mean
median
mode
range

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** median. At the crossing point the number of items below the value equals the number above it, so the value divides the series into two equal halves, which is the median. The mean and the mode are not read from this point.

questions.stem_md: In an arithmetic line graph (time series graph) of the yearly sales of an imagined firm, the usual arrangement of axes is

options.text_md: time on the horizontal axis and sales on the vertical axis
sales on the horizontal axis and time on the vertical axis
class marks on the horizontal axis and frequencies on the vertical axis
cumulative frequencies on both axes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** time on the horizontal axis and sales on the vertical axis. A time series graph places time on the x-axis and the variable on the y-axis, and the points are joined in time order. The other pairings belong to other diagrams or are not used.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The angles of all the sectors of a pie diagram add up to 360 degrees.

**Reason (R):** The sectors together make up the whole circle, which stands for the total of all the components.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Each sector is a share of the circle, and the shares of the total add up to the whole, so the angles must fill the full 360 degrees.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The rectangles of a histogram of a continuous series touch one another.

**Reason (R):** The bars of a simple bar diagram are kept apart by equal gaps.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A is true because continuous classes follow each other without a break; R is a separate rule for a different diagram.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A percentage component bar diagram suits a comparison of how the make-up of totals of different sizes varies.

**Reason (R):** In it every bar has the same height and its parts show shares in per cent of that bar's total.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. When all bars stand for 100 per cent, the difference in the size of the totals is removed and only the make-up is compared.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The less than and more than ogives of a series cross at the median.

**Reason (R):** At the crossing point the cumulative frequency of each ogive is half the total frequency.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. The value at which the items below equal the items above, each half of the total, is the median, and that is the point where the two curves meet.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a time series graph the points are plotted with time on the horizontal axis.

**Reason (R):** A time series graph is drawn by plotting class frequencies against the lower limits of classes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false, because plotting frequencies against class limits is how frequency diagrams and ogives are drawn; a time series graph plots the variable against time periods.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a simple bar diagram, a larger value is shown by making its bar wider.

**Reason (R):** Only the height of a bar carries meaning in a simple bar diagram.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: bars of a simple bar diagram are equally wide and the value is shown by height. R is true, and it is the reason A is wrong.

questions.stem_md: True or false? For the imagined Sunrise Cafe, the sector angles of ingredients, wages, rent, other costs come out as 162°, 108°, 54°, 36°, which add up to 360°.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** 162 + 108 + 54 + 36 = 360, so the statement is true.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the class intervals of a continuous series have unequal widths, the heights of the histogram rectangles can simply be the class frequencies.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** With unequal widths the heights must be adjusted frequencies, so that area stays proportional to frequency; raw frequencies would exaggerate the wide classes.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A well-made table states the source of its figures, usually in a note below the table.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The source note tells the reader where the data came from and lets the figures be checked, so it is part of a complete table.

questions.stem_md: The headings of the rows of a table are called ___ and the headings of its columns are called ___.
questions.solution_md: Row headings are stubs, and column headings are captions.

questions.stem_md: The sector angles of a pie diagram always add up to ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: Together the sectors fill the whole circle, which is 360 degrees.

questions.stem_md: The less than ogive and the more than ogive of a series intersect at the value of its ___.
questions.solution_md: The crossing point marks the median of the series.

questions.stem_md: Match each part of a table with what it does.

options.text_md: Caption
Stub
Source note
Unit of measurement

match_right.text_md: Tells in what terms the figures are expressed, such as thousand tonnes
Tells where the figures were obtained

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Captions head the columns and stubs head the rows; the source note names the origin of the data; the unit states how the figures are measured.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined presentation task with the diagram that suits it best.

options.text_md: Showing how the five heads share a college's annual budget
Showing how many parcels were delivered within 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 hours
Showing the number of labourers in each wage class of a kiln
Showing the yearly sales of a firm over eight years

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Shares of a total call for a pie; cumulative counts for a limit call for an ogive; a continuous frequency distribution is a histogram; values over time are a line graph.

Work out the angle of each component as its share of the total times 360 degrees
Draw a circle and mark a starting radius
Add the amounts to get the total

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The total comes first, then the angles; the circle is drawn and the sectors are marked off one after another.

Plot each cumulative frequency against the upper limit of its class
Add the frequencies successively to get cumulative frequencies
Write the classes with their frequencies

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). Cumulative frequencies can be found only after the table of frequencies exists, and they must be found before plotting and joining.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Sunrise Cafe spends Rs 60,000 a month: ingredients Rs 27,000, wages Rs 18,000, rent Rs 9,000, other costs Rs 6,000. In a pie diagram of these costs, find the angle of the sector for wages.
A pie diagram of the Rs 45,000 fund of the imagined Harsh Valley School shows the sector for sports as 72°. Find the amount spent on sports in rupees.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The sector is 72 ÷ 360 of the circle.
Step 2: Amount = (72 ÷ 360) × 45000 = 9000 rupees.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined district of Devgarh the Central block grew 36, 45, 15, 24 thousand tonnes of wheat, rice, pulses, oilseeds respectively. In a percentage component bar for this block, what share does rice have, in per cent?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Total for the block = 36 + 45 + 15 + 24 = 120.
Step 2: Rice share = 45 ÷ 120 × 100 = 37.5 per cent.

questions.stem_md: The 150 households of the imagined Ashoka Colony are grouped by monthly electricity use (units): 0 to 100: 24; 100 to 200: 30; 200 to 400: 52; 400 to 800: 44. Taking the lowest class width as the standard, find the adjusted frequency of the class 200 to 400.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Width of 200 to 400 = 200; lowest width = 100.
Step 2: Adjusted frequency = 52 ÷ 200 × 100 = 26.

questions.stem_md: Waiting times (minutes) of 50 patients at the imagined Rajpur clinic: 0 to 5: 5; 5 to 10: 10; 10 to 15: 20; 15 to 20: 10; 20 to 25: 5. How many patients waited less than 15 minutes?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Add the frequencies of the classes below 15 minutes: 5 + 10 + 20.
Step 2: The less than cumulative frequency at 15 is 35 patients.

questions.stem_md: Use the waiting-time series of the imagined Rajpur clinic (0 to 5: 5; 5 to 10: 10; 10 to 15: 20; 15 to 20: 10; 20 to 25: 5). Find the more than cumulative frequency at the lower limit 15 minutes.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Patients waiting less than 15 minutes = 35.
Step 2: More than at 15 = 50 − 35 = 15 patients.

questions.stem_md: The two ogives of the imagined Rajpur clinic waiting times (0 to 5: 5; 5 to 10: 10; 10 to 15: 20; 15 to 20: 10; 20 to 25: 5) cross at the median. Find the median waiting time in minutes from the cumulative frequencies.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: N ÷ 2 = 50 ÷ 2 = 25; cumulative frequencies are 5, 15, 35, 45, 50, so the median class is 10 to 15 with cf before it = 15 and f = 20.
Step 2: Median = 10 + (25 − 15) ÷ 20 × 5 = 12.5 minutes.

questions.stem_md: The daily output of the imagined Anand Bolt Works is grouped in classes 50 to 60, 60 to 70, 70 to 80, 80 to 90, 90 to 100, 100 to 110, 110 to 120 crates. To close the frequency polygon on the right, an imaginary class of the same width is added after the last class. Find its class mark.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The last class is 110 to 120, so the imaginary class is 120 to 130.
Step 2: Its class mark = (120 + 130) ÷ 2 = 125 crates.

questions.stem_md: Yearly sales of the imagined Neel Cycles, in units, from 2019 to 2023: 320, 360, 340, 400, 480. Read from the line graph, by what percentage did sales in 2023 exceed those of 2019?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Increase = 480 − 320 = 160 units.
Step 2: Percentage increase = 160 ÷ 320 × 100 = 50 per cent.

questions.stem_md: A table of the imagined Pinewood School shows the members of three clubs of Class 11. The column total is 74 students; two of the three entries are 18 and 26. Find the missing entry.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sum of the known entries = 18 + 26 = 44.
Step 2: Missing entry = 74 − 44 = 30 students.

questions.stem_md: Name the three forms of presenting data and state one use of the tabular form.
questions.solution_md: Three forms named, one use of tables.

answer.model_answer_md: The three forms are **textual (descriptive)**, **tabular** and **diagrammatic** presentation. A table arranges figures in rows and columns, so that related figures can be compared and totals read at a glance.

questions.stem_md: In a table of crop output of the imagined Devgarh district with the crops down the left and the blocks across the top, which are the stubs and which are the captions?
questions.solution_md: Stubs are the row headings and captions are the column headings.

answer.model_answer_md: The **stubs** are the row headings, here the names of the crops (wheat, rice, pulses and oilseeds). The **captions** are the column headings, here the names of the blocks (North, Central and South).

questions.stem_md: Why does a table state the unit of measurement, and what is a footnote used for?
questions.solution_md: Purpose of the unit and of a footnote.

answer.model_answer_md: The **unit** (such as thousand tonnes or rupees) tells the reader how to read every figure, so it is stated above the table or beside the headings. A **footnote** explains a particular entry or exception, for example that a figure is provisional.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish qualitative classification from quantitative classification with an imagined example of each.
questions.solution_md: Attribute versus measurable size, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Qualitative** classification groups items by an attribute that cannot be measured in numbers, such as the trade of workers in an imagined mill. **Quantitative** classification groups them by the size of a measurable variable, such as the monthly wages of those workers in class intervals.

questions.stem_md: A table gives the wheat output of three imagined villages for each of five years. State the temporal classification and the spatial classification found in it.
questions.solution_md: Years are temporal; villages are spatial.

answer.model_answer_md: The classification **by years** is **temporal**, since the data are arranged by time. The classification **by villages** is **spatial** (geographical), since the data are arranged by place.

questions.stem_md: State two rules to be followed while drawing the bars of a bar diagram. Why must they be followed?
questions.solution_md: Equal width and equal gaps; reason is that only height carries meaning.

answer.model_answer_md: The bars must have **equal width** and **equal gaps** between them. Then only the **height** of a bar changes, so a reader compares values by height and is not misled by differences in width or spacing.

questions.stem_md: A student wants to show both the total crop output of each block of Devgarh and how each total divides among the crops. Should she use a multiple bar or a component bar diagram? Give a reason.
questions.solution_md: Component bar shows the total and its parts together.

answer.model_answer_md: A **component (sub-divided) bar diagram**. Each bar's full height shows the block total, and its stacked segments show the crops that make up that total. A multiple bar would show the crops side by side but not the total as a single bar.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: total and parts in one bar

questions.stem_md: The imagined Orchard Club receives Rs 8,000 for its library: books Rs 4,000 and journals Rs 2,500, the rest going to furniture and repairs. Find the pie angles for books and for journals.
questions.solution_md: Angles 180° and 112.5°.

answer.model_answer_md: The angle of a sector is the share of the component in the total, multiplied by 360°. Books: 4000 ÷ 8000 × 360° = **180°**. Journals: 2500 ÷ 8000 × 360° = **112.5°**. The remaining two heads share the rest of the circle.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between a histogram and a bar diagram.
questions.solution_md: Touching versus separate; area versus height.

answer.model_answer_md: A **histogram** has rectangles **touching each other**, because it shows a continuous series, and its **area** represents frequency. A **bar diagram** has **separate bars of equal width** and only the height carries meaning.

questions.stem_md: How is a frequency polygon drawn from a series of equal classes, and how is it closed at both ends?
questions.solution_md: Class marks against frequencies, joined; closed with zero-frequency classes.

answer.model_answer_md: Plot the **class mark** of each class against its **frequency** and join the points by straight lines. To close it, add an **imaginary class with zero frequency** at each end and bring the line down to the class marks of those classes on the axis.

questions.stem_md: Name any three parts of a table and say what each shows, using a table of crop output of an imagined district as your example.
questions.solution_md: Any three parts, each with its role.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Title:** says what the data are, where and when, for example Crop output by block, Devgarh district.
2. **Captions and stubs:** column and row headings, here the block names and the crop names.
3. **Unit and source note:** the unit (thousand tonnes) says how to read the figures, and the source note says where they came from.

questions.stem_md: Compare a simple bar diagram with a pie diagram on what is shown, how the values are read and when each is suited.
questions.solution_md: Three points of comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **What is shown:** a bar diagram shows the size of each item; a pie shows each part as a share of one total.
2. **Reading:** in a bar the value is read from height; in a pie from the angle of a sector, worked out as value ÷ total × 360°.
3. **Suitability:** bars suit comparing many items or separate totals; a pie suits a few components of a single total.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Naidu family spends Rs 36,000 a month: food Rs 14,400, rent Rs 9,000, education Rs 5,400, savings Rs 3,600, other items Rs 3,600. Find the angles of the sectors for food, rent and savings in a pie diagram.
questions.solution_md: Angles 144°, 90° and 36°.

answer.model_answer_md: The total is 36000, and each angle is the amount divided by the total and multiplied by 360°. Food: 14400 ÷ 36000 × 360° = **144°**. Rent: 9000 ÷ 36000 × 360° = **90°**. Savings: 3600 ÷ 36000 × 360° = **36°**. The other two heads fill the rest of the circle.

questions.stem_md: A table of the imagined Ashoka Colony groups 150 households by electricity units: 0 to 100: 24; 100 to 200: 30; 200 to 400: 52; 400 to 800: 44. Find the adjusted frequencies for a histogram with the lowest width as the standard.

answer.model_answer_md: The widths are 100, 100, 200, 400, so the standard is 100. Adjusted frequencies: 24 ÷ 100 × 100 = 24; 30 ÷ 100 × 100 = 30; 52 ÷ 200 × 100 = 26; 44 ÷ 400 × 100 = 11. These are the heights of the rectangles.

questions.stem_md: The delivery times (hours) of 50 parcels of the imagined Sunbeam Courier have cumulative less than frequencies 6, 20, 40, 48, 50 at the upper limits 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Explain why the two ogives meet at the median, and state the value of the cumulative frequency where they meet.
questions.solution_md: Equal numbers below and above; cumulative frequency 25; median 4.5 hours.

answer.model_answer_md: At the meeting point the number of parcels below the delivery time equals the number above it, so the value splits the 50 parcels into two equal halves, which is the median. Each ogive then shows 50 ÷ 2 = **25** parcels, and the median is 4.5 hours.

marking_scheme.step: Cumulative frequency at the crossing computed

questions.stem_md: Yearly sales of the imagined Neel Cycles in units for 2019 to 2023 are 320, 360, 340, 400, 480. Describe how to draw its arithmetic line graph and state the year in which sales fell.
questions.solution_md: Axes, plotting and joining, and the year of fall, 2021.

answer.model_answer_md: Mark **time (years)** on the horizontal axis and **sales (units)** on the vertical axis, with a convenient scale and a title. Plot a point for each year and join the points with straight lines in order of time. The line slopes downward only once: sales fell in **2021**, from 360 to 340 units.

questions.stem_md: The weekly market of the imagined village of Hariharpur sold 120 kg of tomatoes, 90 kg of onions, 60 kg of potatoes on Tuesday, and 150 kg of tomatoes, 110 kg of onions, 75 kg of potatoes on Friday. Present these facts as a table with row and column totals, and name the parts you have used.

|---|---|---|---|---|

questions.stem_md: Describe the simple, multiple and component bar diagrams, saying what each shows. Also explain how the percentage form of the component bar diagram is useful.
questions.solution_md: Three types described, the rule on bars, and the use of the percentage form.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **simple bar diagram** shows one series, such as the yearly output of one crop, with one bar for each item.
2. A **multiple (grouped) bar diagram** puts two or more related series side by side for each item, for comparison.
3. A **component (sub-divided) bar diagram** divides each bar into parts that show the components of its total.
4. In every case the bars have **equal width and equal gaps**; only height carries meaning.
5. The **percentage component bar** makes every bar 100 per cent, so the make-up of totals of unequal size can be compared directly.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Lakshya Coaching Institute has a monthly budget of Rs 50,000: rent Rs 20,000, salaries Rs 15,000, power and internet Rs 5,000, stationery Rs 5,000, other items Rs 5,000. Compute the sector angles for a pie diagram, show that they add up correctly and describe how the diagram is drawn.

answer.model_answer_md: The total is 50000, so angle = amount ÷ 50000 × 360°. Rent: 20000 ÷ 50000 × 360° = **144°**; Salaries: 15000 ÷ 50000 × 360° = **108°**; Power and internet: 5000 ÷ 50000 × 360° = **36°**; Stationery: 5000 ÷ 50000 × 360° = **36°**; Other items: 5000 ÷ 50000 × 360° = **36°**. Check: 144 + 108 + 36 + 36 + 36 = **360°**, the full circle. To draw the diagram, make a circle, mark a starting radius, and with a protractor mark off the sectors in turn, then label each with its head and angle.

questions.stem_md: The monthly water bills (rupees) of 108 households of the imagined Gulmohar Residents' Association are grouped as 0 to 100: 16; 100 to 200: 24; 200 to 400: 36; 400 to 800: 32. Find the heights for a histogram, and say how a frequency polygon would be added.
questions.solution_md: Heights 16, 24, 18, 8; polygon by joining mid-points.

answer.model_answer_md: Widths are 100, 100, 200, 400; the standard width is 100. Adjusted frequencies: 16 ÷ 100 × 100 = 16; 24 ÷ 100 × 100 = 24; 36 ÷ 200 × 100 = 18; 32 ÷ 400 × 100 = 8. Draw touching rectangles of these heights. For the **polygon**, join the mid-points of the tops of the rectangles with straight lines, and extend the ends to the axis at the class marks of imaginary classes.

questions.stem_md: The delivery times (hours) of 50 parcels of the imagined Sunbeam Courier are 0 to 2: 6; 2 to 4: 14; 4 to 6: 20; 6 to 8: 8; 8 to 10: 2. Give the less than and more than cumulative frequencies, and show how the two ogives give the median.
questions.solution_md: Cumulative frequencies listed; ogives cross at 25 and 4.5 hours.

answer.model_answer_md: Less than cumulative frequencies at the upper limits: 2: 6; 4: 20; 6: 40; 8: 48; 10: 50. More than cumulative frequencies at the lower limits: 0: 50; 2: 44; 4: 30; 6: 10; 8: 2. Plot the less than points against upper limits and the more than points against lower limits on one graph, and join each set smoothly. The curves cross at a cumulative frequency of 50 ÷ 2 = **25**, and the value on the x-axis below that point is the median, **4.5 hours**.

questions.stem_md: Compare textual, tabular and diagrammatic presentation of data, stating a merit and a limit of each, and say when you would choose each.
questions.solution_md: Three forms with merits and limits, and a choice rule.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Textual:** data in sentences. Merit: suits a few figures and brings in explanation. Limit: many figures become hard to follow.
2. **Tabular:** rows and columns. Merit: precise figures, easy comparison and totals. Limit: a long table can tire the eye.
3. **Diagrammatic:** bars, pies, graphs. Merit: striking, shows pattern at a glance. Limit: exact values are hard to read.
4. Choose text for a few facts, a table for exact figures and a diagram to show a pattern to a wide audience.
